blocks.text: **COPD** is a preventable and treatable disease defined by **persistent airflow limitation**. The limitation usually gets worse over time and comes from an exaggerated, long-lasting inflammatory reaction of the airways and lung tissue to inhaled noxious particles or gases. In any one patient, exacerbations and comorbid diseases add to the overall severity. Kumar describes COPD as an **umbrella diagnosis** that unites emphysema, small airways disease and chronic bronchitis, all sharing airflow limitation that does not fully reverse.

blocks.title: The two older labels inside COPD
rows: Cough productive of sputum for **≥ 3 months a year in 2 consecutive years**, once other causes of chronic cough are excluded
Permanent, abnormal widening of the airspaces beyond the terminal bronchioles, with destruction of their walls and no obvious fibrosis

blocks.title: Risk factors
items: **Tobacco smoking**: the dominant cause (about 95% of UK cases in Davidson). Risk rises with both amount and duration.
COPD is **unusual below 10 pack-years** (1 pack-year = 20 cigarettes a day for 1 year). Not every smoker develops it, so individual susceptibility matters.
Indoor smoke from **biomass fuel** used for cooking in confined spaces
Occupational dusts: **coal dust, silica, cadmium**
Early life: low birth weight, and poor lung growth in childhood (infections, maternal smoking)
Recurrent infections; **HIV** (linked to emphysema); low socioeconomic status; cannabis
Host factors: **alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency** and airway hyper-reactivity

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis.** Smoke draws neutrophils, macrophages and CD8+ T cells into the airways. Neutrophils release **elastases and proteases**, and smoke also inactivates alpha1-antitrypsin. The result is a **protease–antiprotease imbalance** that digests alveolar walls (emphysema). Separately, constant irritation of the large airways causes **mucous gland hypertrophy and more goblet cells**, which produce the sputum of chronic bronchitis.

blocks.title: Patterns of emphysema
rows: Around the respiratory bronchioles; distal alveoli relatively spared
The whole acinus; severe cases become a collection of bullae
Patchy damage that ignores acinar structure

blocks.text: **Alpha1-antitrypsin** is made in the liver and travels to the lung, where it blocks **neutrophil elastase**. Main phenotypes: **MM** normal, **MZ** heterozygous deficiency, **ZZ** homozygous deficiency. Inherited deficiency causes about **2% of UK emphysema** and can also cause liver disease, because the abnormal protein builds up in hepatocytes.

blocks.note: Look at: normal lung beside emphysematous lung. Note the large airspaces and the loss of gas-exchange surface.
Look at: PAS-stained bronchial mucosa with an increased number of mucus-secreting goblet cells (the chronic bronchitis component).

blocks.text: **Basal, pan-acinar emphysema in a young patient or a lifelong non-smoker** points to alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency. Check the serum level and the genotype.

Think of COPD in **anyone over 40** with chronic bronchitic symptoms and/or breathlessness, typically a long-term smoker. A productive **"smoker's cough"** is usually the first symptom. **Breathlessness** is what usually brings the patient to a doctor. Wheeze and recurrent chest infections, often worse in winter, are common. Main differentials: **chronic asthma, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis and congestive cardiac failure**.

blocks.title: Modified MRC dyspnoea scale (Davidson)
rows: When hurrying on the flat or walking up a slight hill
Walks slower than people of the same age on the flat, or has to stop when walking at own pace
Stops for breath after about 100 m or a few minutes on the flat
Too breathless to leave the house, or breathless when dressing

blocks.text: **Two numbering systems.** Davidson's _modified_ MRC scale runs **0–4**. The NICE MRC scale quoted in Zero to Finals runs **1–5**, so "stops after 100 m" is grade 3 in one and grade 4 in the other. Read the scale the question names.

blocks.title: Signs
items: **Mild disease:** often no signs, or only quiet wheeze

**Severe disease:** tachypnoea, **prolonged expiration**, **pursed-lip breathing** (splints the airways open), accessory muscle use (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes), intercostal indrawing, tripod posture
**Hyperinflation:** barrel chest, **reduced cricosternal distance**, poor expansion, hyper-resonance, **loss of cardiac and liver dullness**
Quiet breath sounds; crackles may come with infection
**CO2 retention:** warm peripheries (vasodilatation), bounding pulse, **coarse flapping tremor**; confusion and drowsiness when severe
Advanced disease: ask about **ankle oedema** and **morning headaches**, which suggest hypercapnia

blocks.title: Classic phenotypes (in practice they overlap)
rows: Productive cough, **secondary polycythaemia**, signs of right heart strain

blocks.note: Look at: thin patient with muscle wasting, pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, leaning forward and accessory muscle use.

blocks.text: **Finger clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD.** If present, look for **lung cancer or fibrosis**. Crackles that persist between infections suggest **bronchiectasis**. Haemoptysis or chest pain must not be blamed on COPD without investigation.

Signs are non-specific, appear late and correlate poorly with lung function. A barrel chest can come from **spinal osteoporosis** in older men, and centri-acinar emphysema can exist with no signs of hyperinflation.

The diagnosis needs **objective proof of airflow obstruction on spirometry**: a **post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 (70%)**. Severity is then graded by the **post-bronchodilator FEV1 as % predicted**.

blocks.title: Spirometric severity (all require FEV1/FVC < 0.7)
rows: **≥ 80%** (do not diagnose on spirometry alone if asymptomatic)

blocks.title: Reading the tests
items: Volume–time trace: slow, prolonged, limited exhalation; FEV1 falls **out of proportion** to FVC
Flow–volume loop: **scooped (coved) expiratory limb** as intrathoracic airways collapse in mid and late expiration
Lung volumes: **raised RV and TLC** (gas trapping, hyperinflation), most marked in emphysema
In severe COPD or with large bullae, use **body plethysmography**, because helium dilution under-estimates lung volumes
**Low gas transfer suggests emphysema**; gas transfer is normal in pure chronic bronchitis

blocks.text: **Reversibility.** After a short-acting β2-agonist, a rise of **> 12% and > 200 mL** in FEV1 or FVC counts as significant reversibility. A **large rise (> 400 mL)** together with variable peak flow points to **asthma** rather than COPD.

blocks.title: Other baseline tests
items: **Chest X-ray:** no reliable sign of severity and often normal even in advanced disease, but **essential to exclude heart failure and lung cancer** and to find bullae. Classic film: hyperinflation, **low flat diaphragms**, long narrow heart, **pruned peripheral vessels** with large proximal vessels.
**HRCT:** quantifies emphysema, beats the CXR for **bullae**, and guides lung volume reduction surgery
**FBC:** anaemia, or **secondary polycythaemia**
**Alpha1-antitrypsin level (± genotype):** young patients with basal emphysema, premature disease, lifelong non-smokers, family history
**ECG:** often normal. With pulmonary hypertension: **P pulmonale**, RBBB, RV hypertrophy. **Echo** if breathlessness is out of proportion.
**Pulse oximetry < 93%** → refer for home oxygen assessment. Baseline BMI and sputum culture are also useful.

blocks.text: **BODE index** predicts mortality: **B**MI, airflow **O**bstruction (FEV1), **D**yspnoea (MRC) and **E**xercise capacity (6-minute walk). A score of 0–2 carries about **10%** mortality at 52 months, versus about **80%** for 7–10.

blocks.note: Look at: COPD volume–time trace (slow, prolonged exhalation) and the scooped expiratory flow–volume loop, compared with fibrosis and large-airway obstruction.
Look at: the scooped expiratory limb of obstruction compared with the small, narrow loop of restriction.
Look at: HRCT with gross emphysema (large low-density areas), most marked in the right lower lobe.
Look at: CXR with hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms and an enlarged retrosternal air space.

blocks.text: An **acute exacerbation** is a worsening of symptoms with a fall in lung function and health status. In practice that means **more breathlessness, more sputum, or sputum that becomes purulent**. Exacerbations become **more frequent as the disease advances**. They can bring on **respiratory failure and/or fluid retention**, and they are an important cause of death.

blocks.title: Precipitants
items: **Infection** is the main trigger. **Viruses** cause many episodes. Bacteria: _Strep. pneumoniae_, _H. influenzae_, _Moraxella catarrhalis_ (± _Mycoplasma_).
**Change in air quality** (pollution)
**Non-adherence** to maintenance therapy
**Cardiac disease**, e.g. heart failure
Mimics to **exclude**: **pneumothorax** (bullae), **pulmonary embolism**, heart failure
**Excess oxygen** in a CO2 retainer can tip compensated type II failure into acidosis

blocks.text: **Acute on chronic type II failure.** COPD is the commonest cause of **chronic type II respiratory failure**. PaCO2 is high, but the **kidneys retain bicarbonate**, so pH stays normal. An exacerbation adds an acute CO2 load that the kidneys cannot match, so **pH falls** ("acute on chronic"): first respiratory distress, then drowsiness and coma.

blocks.title: Arterial blood gas interpretation
rows: Low PaO2, normal or low PaCO2
pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa after initial treatment

blocks.title: Investigations in an exacerbation
items: **ABG: mandatory** (hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, pH, bicarbonate); repeat after changes in oxygen or treatment
**CXR:** look for **pneumothorax** (needs a drain, possibly CT-guided in bullous disease) or **pneumonia** (antibiotics)
**ECG:** arrhythmia, right heart strain
**FBC** (white cells), **U&E**
**Sputum culture** if infection is significant; **blood cultures** if septic
Get an ABG whenever SpO2 is below 92% or consciousness is reduced

blocks.text: Patients in acute on chronic type II failure **may not look distressed despite being critically ill**. Judge severity by the **ABG**, not by appearance.
Not every acute worsening in COPD is an infective exacerbation. **Pneumothorax, PE and heart failure** produce the same picture and must be actively excluded (CXR, ECG, clinical context).

blocks.note: Look at: the exacerbation algorithm. CXR (pneumothorax → drain; pneumonia → antibiotics), then ABG, then Venturi oxygen to 88–92%, then NIV if pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa.

blocks.text: The aims are to **ease breathlessness**, **reduce how often and how badly exacerbations happen**, and improve health status and prognosis.

**Smoking cessation is the only measure that changes the natural history.** After stopping, FEV1 declines at the never-smoker rate again, but lost function does not come back. Only **stopping smoking and LTOT** have consistently been shown to lower mortality.

blocks.title: Drug options
rows: As-needed relief; enough for mild disease
Regular use in moderate–severe disease. Breathlessness may improve with little FEV1 change (less dynamic hyperinflation).
A LAMA does **not** slow FEV1 decline. Use LAMAs with caution in significant heart disease or urinary retention.
Better lung function and quality of life, **fewer exacerbations**. Used for frequent exacerbations or FEV1 < 50%; **blood eosinophilia predicts benefit**.
**More pneumonia**, especially in the elderly; avoid high-dose ICS
May cut exacerbations in frequent exacerbators
Davidson: evidence of benefit is limited
Side-effects, erratic metabolism and interactions, so **monitor levels**

blocks.title: NICE-style escalation (Zero to Finals)
items: Step 1: SABA or SAMA as needed
Step 2, **no** asthmatic or steroid-responsive features: **LABA + LAMA**
Step 2, asthmatic or steroid-responsive features: **LABA + ICS**
Step 3: LABA + LAMA + ICS
Severe disease: add nebulisers, theophylline, carbocisteine, prophylactic azithromycin, LTOT

blocks.text: **Avoid maintenance oral glucocorticoids**: they cause osteoporosis and skeletal muscle weakness. A trial of oral steroids helps diagnose asthma but **does not predict** whether inhaled steroids will help in COPD.

blocks.title: Pulmonary rehabilitation
items: Exercise training, education and nutritional advice, delivered by a multidisciplinary team
Usually **2–3 sessions a week for 6–12 weeks**
Sustained gains in **exercise tolerance and health status**; patients learn that breathlessness is not dangerous

blocks.title: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT), Davidson
rows: Clinically stable on optimal therapy; **two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart**
**PaO2 < 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg)** whatever the PaCO2, with FEV1 < 1.5 L
**PaO2 7.3–8 kPa** plus pulmonary hypertension, peripheral oedema or nocturnal hypoxaemia (Kumar and Essentials also list secondary polycythaemia)
**≥ 15 h/day** (more benefit at > 20 h) at 2–4 L/min, aiming for PaO2 > 8 kPa / SaO2 ≥ 90%. **Improves survival.**

blocks.text: **LTOT hours differ between books.** Davidson: at least 15 h/day, with more benefit above 20 h. Kumar & Clark Essentials: 19 h/day at 1–3 L/min. US sources (Pocket Medicine) use PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤ 89%. For this course, follow Davidson.

blocks.title: Surgery, other measures and palliation
items: **Bullectomy:** large bullae compressing normal lung

**Lung volume reduction surgery:** upper-lobe emphysema with preserved gas transfer and no pulmonary hypertension. Kumar notes a controlled trial in severe emphysema with _higher_ mortality, so careful selection is key.
**Lung transplantation:** selected patients with advanced disease
**Venesection** if the packed cell volume is > 55%
Address obesity, poor nutrition, depression and social isolation
Palliation: **morphine** for breathlessness, **low-dose benzodiazepine** for anxiety; discuss resuscitation early

blocks.text: **Role of vaccination.** Infections are the commonest trigger of exacerbations, so prevention is part of routine care. Offer **influenza vaccine every year** plus **pneumococcal vaccination**. Davidson says pneumococcal "as appropriate". Kumar gives a single dose of the polyvalent polysaccharide vaccine. Step-Up offers it to all adults with COPD (once before 65 and once after).

blocks.note: Look at: accelerated FEV1 decline in a susceptible smoker. After stopping at 45 or 65 the curve returns to the normal slope, but the lost function is not regained.

blocks.text: Many patients can stay **at home** with more bronchodilator, a **short course of oral steroid** and, where indicated, antibiotics. **Cyanosis, peripheral oedema or altered consciousness** call for hospital referral. Comorbidities and social circumstances also weigh in.

blocks.title: Hospital treatment
rows: Davidson: PaO2 > 8 kPa / SaO2 > 90% without worsening acidosis. BTS (Kumar): **SpO2 88–92%** if at risk of hypercapnia. High-flow O2 can depress breathing.
If the patient is oxygen-sensitive, drive the nebuliser with **air** and give O2 by nasal cannula
**Oral prednisolone 30 mg for 10 days** (shorter courses acceptable)
Consider bone protection with repeated courses
If sputum purulence, sputum volume or breathlessness increases: **aminopenicillin, tetracycline or macrolide**
**Co-amoxiclav** only where β-lactamase producers are common
Mild–moderate **respiratory acidosis: pH < 7.35 (H+ ≥ 45 nmol/L)** with raised PaCO2
Start early: fewer intubations, treatment failures and deaths. **Not** if the patient cannot protect the airway.
Physiotherapy for secretions; **diuretics** for oedema; LMWH thromboprophylaxis
IV aminophylline: weak evidence, risk of arrhythmia. Doxapram largely replaced by NIV.

blocks.title: NIV limits and escalation
items: Contraindications: altered mental state, cannot cooperate or clear secretions, haemodynamic instability, upper GI bleeding
**Intubate** if PaCO2 or respiratory rate keeps rising, pH keeps falling or the patient tires
Invasive ventilation is most reasonable when there is a **reversible cause** (e.g. pneumonia) or no previous respiratory failure. Agree a ceiling of care early.

blocks.text: Venturi masks are **fixed-performance** devices: entrained air gives a predictable FiO2 (24%, 28%, 35%…). UK colour code: **24% blue, 28% white**.

**Antibiotics: the books disagree.** Davidson finds little evidence for routine antibiotics and gives them only when sputum purulence, sputum volume or breathlessness increases. Kumar says to give them promptly in every acute episode and supports home "rescue packs". **Follow Davidson.**

**Steroid course length differs.** Davidson: prednisolone **30 mg for 10 days** (shorter is acceptable). Zero to Finals: 30–40 mg in hospital. Pocket Medicine: 40 mg for 5 days. Exacerbations need **systemic** steroids; inhaled steroids are maintenance drugs and cannot replace them.

**Why oxygen raises CO2.** Davidson and Kumar say chronic retainers lose sensitivity to CO2 and come to depend on hypoxic drive. Step-Up blames worsening V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect instead. Either way the exam answer is the same: **controlled oxygen with ABG monitoring**.

blocks.note: Look at: Venturi (fixed-performance) mask, with the jet and air-entrainment ports that set the oxygen percentage.

blocks.title: Pulmonary manifestations
rows: Mucous gland enlargement, more goblet cells
Loss of elastic tissue, airway wall inflammation and fibrosis
Premature airway closure, **gas trapping, dynamic hyperinflation**
Respiratory muscles at a mechanical disadvantage, so **work of breathing rises** (first on exercise, then at rest)
Alveolar destruction (**emphysema**), less gas-exchange surface, bullae
Impaired cardiac performance; **pulmonary hypertension** and cor pulmonale in later stages

blocks.title: Extrapulmonary (systemic) effects and comorbidities
items: **Weight loss** (altered fat metabolism) and malnutrition; BMI carries prognostic weight
**Skeletal muscle weakness** (deconditioning, inflammation, hypoxia) that limits exercise independently of lung function
Raised circulating inflammatory markers
**Osteoporosis**
**Salt and water retention**, causing peripheral oedema
**Depression and anxiety**
Comorbidities: cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, **lung cancer**

blocks.title: Complications
items: Recurrent **exacerbations**
**Chronic type II respiratory failure** (COPD is its commonest cause): chronic respiratory acidosis with compensatory bicarbonate retention
**Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale**: raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, oedema
**Secondary polycythaemia** from chronic hypoxaemia (Hct > 55% in men, > 47% in women); venesect if PCV > 55%
**Bullae and pneumothorax**
Lung cancer or TB: new **fatigue, anorexia and weight loss** should raise suspicion

blocks.text: Right heart failure can occur in advanced COPD, but **pitting oedema is often due to renal salt and water retention** from hypoxia and hypercapnia, with no heart failure. In those patients "cor pulmonale" is a **misnomer**.
**Poor prognosis:** older age, low post-bronchodilator FEV1, weight loss, pulmonary hypertension. Common modes of death: **respiratory failure, cardiac disease and lung cancer**.

blocks.note: Look at: the map of pulmonary features (glands, airway fibrosis, emphysema, vascular remodelling) and systemic features (muscle weakness, oedema, osteoporosis, weight loss).

cards.front: Chronic bronchitis: clinical definition?
cards.back: Productive cough for ≥ 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years (other causes excluded)

cards.front: Which emphysema pattern is seen in alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency, and where?
cards.back: **Pan-acinar** (panlobular), predominantly in the **lung bases**

cards.front: Below how many pack-years is COPD unusual?
cards.back: **10 pack-years** (1 pack-year = 20 cigarettes/day for 1 year)

cards.front: Finger clubbing in a COPD patient means?
cards.back: Not part of COPD. Look for **lung cancer or fibrosis**.

cards.front: Signs of CO2 retention?
cards.back: Warm peripheries, **bounding pulse**, **coarse flapping tremor**; confusion/drowsiness; morning headaches

cards.front: Spirometric criterion for COPD?
cards.back: **Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.7**

cards.front: FEV1 cut-offs for mild / moderate / severe / very severe COPD?
cards.back: ≥ 80% / 50–79% / 30–49% / < 30% predicted (all with FEV1/FVC < 0.7)

cards.front: Gas transfer (TLCO) in emphysema vs chronic bronchitis?
cards.back: Emphysema: **reduced**. Pure chronic bronchitis: **normal**.

cards.front: Significant bronchodilator reversibility? Which size of rise suggests asthma?
cards.back: > 12% **and** > 200 mL rise in FEV1 or FVC. A rise **> 400 mL** suggests asthma.

cards.front: Bacteria commonly behind infective exacerbations?
cards.back: _Strep. pneumoniae_, _H. influenzae_, _Moraxella catarrhalis_ (many episodes are viral)

cards.front: ABG: chronic vs acute-on-chronic type II failure?
cards.back: Both have high PaCO2 and high HCO3. Chronic: **normal pH**. Acute on chronic: **pH < 7.35**.

cards.front: LTOT criteria (Davidson)?
cards.back: Stable, two ABGs ≥ 3 weeks apart, non-smoker. **PaO2 < 7.3 kPa**, or **7.3–8 kPa** with pulmonary hypertension, oedema or nocturnal hypoxaemia.

cards.front: LTOT: minimum hours and target?
cards.back: **≥ 15 h/day** (better > 20 h) at 2–4 L/min to PaO2 > 8 kPa / SaO2 ≥ 90%

cards.front: Vaccines for every COPD patient?
cards.back: **Annual influenza** + **pneumococcal** vaccination

cards.front: Only measure that changes the natural history of COPD?
cards.back: **Smoking cessation**

cards.front: Target SpO2 and device for a CO2 retainer in an exacerbation?
cards.back: **88–92%** via a **Venturi mask** (start 24–28%)

cards.front: When is NIV indicated in an exacerbation?
cards.back: Respiratory acidosis **pH < 7.35** (PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa) despite initial medical therapy, in a patient who can protect the airway

cards.front: Davidson's steroid course for an exacerbation?
cards.back: Oral **prednisolone 30 mg for 10 days** (shorter acceptable)

cards.front: Ankle oedema in COPD without heart failure: cause?
cards.back: Renal **salt and water retention** from hypoxia and hypercapnia ("cor pulmonale" is a misnomer)

cards.front: Secondary polycythaemia: when to venesect?
cards.back: Packed cell volume **> 55%**

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman who has never smoked has had worsening breathlessness for 2 years. Spirometry shows fixed airflow obstruction. CT shows emphysema mainly in both lower lobes. Her liver enzymes are mildly raised.
questions.leadIn: Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Early, basal (pan-acinar) emphysema in a never-smoker** plus liver involvement is classic **alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency**. The abnormal protein builds up in the liver, so too little reaches the lung to block neutrophil elastase.
whyNot: Asthma does not cause emphysema on CT or abnormal liver enzymes, and its obstruction is usually variable.
Bronchiectasis causes dilated, thick-walled bronchi and chronic purulent sputum, not basal emphysema.
Fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with a normal or high FEV1/FVC, not obstruction with emphysema.
Cystic fibrosis presents earlier with bronchiectasis and pancreatic insufficiency rather than isolated basal emphysema.

questions.stem: A pathology student is studying lung tissue from a heavy smoker with emphysema.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains the destruction of the alveolar walls?
options: Protease–antiprotease imbalance driven by neutrophil elastase
Mucous gland hypertrophy in the large airways
questions.explanation: Smoke recruits neutrophils (and macrophages, CD8+ T cells) that release **elastases and proteases**. Smoke also inactivates alpha1-antitrypsin, and the resulting **protease–antiprotease imbalance** digests alveolar walls.
whyNot: Eosinophilic, CD4+ (Th2) inflammation is the pattern of asthma, not COPD.
Gland hypertrophy explains the sputum of chronic bronchitis, not alveolar destruction.
Emphysema is by definition destruction without obvious fibrosis; honeycombing belongs to pulmonary fibrosis.
Immune-complex disease is not the mechanism of smoking-related emphysema.

questions.theme: Explaining examination findings in patients with COPD
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Renal salt and water retention from hypoxia and hypercapnia

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with known COPD and a 50 pack-year history has developed finger clubbing over the past few months. He has lost 6 kg in weight without trying.
items.explanation: **Clubbing is not a feature of COPD**, so its appearance means another disease. Together with unexplained weight loss in a heavy smoker, **lung cancer** is the leading concern.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD is drowsy on the ward. Her hands are warm, her pulse is bounding and she has a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands.
items.explanation: Warm peripheries (vasodilatation), a bounding pulse and a flapping tremor are the classic signs of **CO2 retention**. Severe hypercapnia also causes drowsiness and confusion.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man with severe COPD has bilateral pitting ankle oedema. His JVP is not raised and echocardiography shows normal right and left ventricular function. On air, PaO2 is 7.0 kPa and PaCO2 is 7.3 kPa.
items.explanation: Two steps: the normal echo and JVP rule out heart failure, so the oedema comes from **renal salt and water retention driven by hypoxia and hypercapnia**. Calling this "cor pulmonale" would be a misnomer.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman labelled with COPD has coarse crackles at both bases that persist between infections. She brings up a cupful of purulent sputum every day.
items.explanation: Crackles that **persist** outside infections, with large daily volumes of purulent sputum, suggest **bronchiectasis** rather than simple COPD.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 59-year-old ex-smoker: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.52, FEV1 45% predicted, TLC 128% predicted, RV raised. TLCO is 40% predicted and KCO is low.
items.explanation: Obstruction plus **hyperinflation** plus **low gas transfer** (TLCO and KCO) means alveolar surface has been lost: **emphysema-predominant** COPD.

items.stem: A 61-year-old smoker has coughed up sputum every winter for many years. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.61, FEV1 63% predicted. TLCO and KCO are normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: the ratio below 0.7 confirms COPD, and the **normal gas transfer** shows the alveoli are preserved. With a long productive-cough history this is the **chronic bronchitis** pattern.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman: FEV1/FVC 0.62. After salbutamol her FEV1 rises by 520 mL (30%). Her home peak-flow diary shows large swings through the day.
items.explanation: A rise of **more than 400 mL** after bronchodilator, with variable peak flow, points to **asthma** rather than COPD.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man: FEV1/FVC 0.88, FVC 58% predicted, TLC reduced, TLCO markedly reduced.
items.explanation: A normal or high ratio with **small lung volumes and low gas transfer** is a restrictive pattern, typical of **pulmonary fibrosis**.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker has exertional breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.58, FEV1 42% predicted. ABG on air is normal.
questions.leadIn: How severe is his airflow obstruction?
questions.explanation: With FEV1/FVC < 0.7, an FEV1 of **30–49% predicted** is **severe** (GOLD/NICE stage 3).
whyNot: Mild requires FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted.
Moderate is FEV1 50–79% predicted.
Very severe is FEV1 < 30%, or < 50% with respiratory failure, and his gases are normal.
A ratio of 0.58 is below 0.7, so obstruction is present.

questions.theme: Arterial blood gas patterns in COPD
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure
Acute type 2 respiratory failure without chronic retention

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD is seen at a routine clinic, feeling his usual self. On air: pH 7.39, PaCO2 7.4 kPa, PaO2 7.6 kPa, HCO3 33 mmol/L.
items.explanation: High PaCO2 with a **normal pH and high bicarbonate**: the kidneys have fully compensated a long-standing CO2 retention.

items.stem: Two months later the same man is admitted with green sputum and worse breathlessness. pH 7.27, PaCO2 9.6 kPa, PaO2 6.8 kPa, HCO3 34 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: the **raised bicarbonate** shows chronic retention, and the **pH < 7.35** shows a fresh CO2 load the kidneys cannot match. This is acute on chronic type 2 failure.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with moderate COPD and right lower lobe pneumonia: pH 7.46, PaCO2 4.1 kPa, PaO2 7.2 kPa, HCO3 24 mmol/L.
items.explanation: A low PaO2 with a **normal or low PaCO2** is **type 1** respiratory failure; she is hyperventilating.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD is brought in by ambulance during an exacerbation. He is drowsy but rousable and does not look distressed.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is essential to judge how severe this episode is?
questions.explanation: In acute on chronic type II failure the patient **may look calm despite being critically ill**. The **ABG** (PaO2, PaCO2, pH, bicarbonate) is mandatory and guides oxygen and NIV.
whyNot: Spirometry diagnoses and stages stable COPD; it says nothing about gas exchange or acidaemia, and a drowsy patient cannot perform it.
HRCT characterises emphysema and bullae; it does not assess acute severity.
Echo assesses cardiac function and is not the key acute severity test.
Sputum culture guides antibiotics later; it does not measure how ill he is.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with COPD has been stable on optimal inhaled therapy. She stopped smoking 2 years ago. Two ABGs on air, taken 3 weeks apart, show PaO2 7.6 kPa and 7.7 kPa. She has ankle oedema.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate oxygen prescription?
options: No oxygen, because PaO2 is above 7.3 kPa
Long-term oxygen for at least 15 hours a day
Short-burst oxygen as needed for breathlessness
questions.explanation: PaO2 **7.3–8 kPa plus peripheral oedema** (or pulmonary hypertension or nocturnal hypoxaemia) meets the LTOT criteria. She is a non-smoker and the gases were confirmed twice, 3 weeks apart. LTOT is given for **≥ 15 h/day**.
whyNot: The 7.3 kPa cut-off applies on its own; between 7.3 and 8 kPa, complications such as oedema still qualify.
Exercise-only oxygen does not provide the hours a day needed for a survival benefit.
Overnight oxygen alone falls short of the 15-hour minimum.
Short-burst oxygen is not LTOT and cannot provide the ≥ 15 h/day linked to the survival benefit.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed moderate COPD asks which single step will do most to change the course of his disease.
questions.leadIn: Which intervention is it?
options: Inhaled steroid with a long-acting β2-agonist
questions.explanation: **Smoking cessation is the only measure that favourably changes the natural history**: FEV1 decline slows to the non-smoker rate.
whyNot: LAMAs improve symptoms and quality of life but do not prevent FEV1 decline.
ICS/LABA reduces exacerbations and improves symptoms but does not alter the natural course.
Rehabilitation improves exercise tolerance and health status, not the rate of FEV1 decline.
Vaccination prevents infective exacerbations but does not change the underlying decline.

questions.theme: Treatment decisions in acute exacerbations of COPD
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Controlled oxygen via a 24% or 28% Venturi mask
High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather reservoir mask

items.stem: A 70-year-old man is treated for an exacerbation with nebulisers, oral steroids and 28% oxygen. One hour later he is alert and cooperative, but his ABG shows pH 7.30 and PaCO2 8.2 kPa.
items.explanation: Persistent **respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35, high PaCO2) despite initial treatment** in a patient who can protect the airway is the indication for **NIV**.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with COPD arrives breathless with SpO2 82% on air. An ABG shows PaCO2 7.9 kPa, pH 7.37 and a raised bicarbonate. What should be the first step in her oxygen treatment?
items.explanation: She is a chronic CO2 retainer (raised bicarbonate, normal pH). Give **controlled oxygen by Venturi mask**, aiming for SpO2 88–92%, to avoid worsening hypercapnia.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with known bullous emphysema suddenly becomes more breathless. The CXR shows a large right pneumothorax.
items.explanation: The CXR step of the exacerbation algorithm finds a **pneumothorax**, which needs a **chest drain** (CT guidance may be needed in complex bullous disease).

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman managed at home has more breathlessness and more sputum, which has turned green. Her GP has already increased her bronchodilator and started oral prednisolone, and now decides what else to add. Beta-lactamase-producing organisms are uncommon locally.
items.explanation: Increased sputum purulence and volume justify antibiotics. Davidson advises a **simple regimen** (aminopenicillin, tetracycline or macrolide); co-amoxiclav is kept for areas where β-lactamase producers are common.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD looks plethoric and complains of headaches. Hb is 205 g/L and packed cell volume is 0.59.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment is indicated for the blood count abnormality?
questions.explanation: Chronic hypoxaemia drives **secondary polycythaemia**. **Venesection** is indicated once the packed cell volume is **above 55%**.
whyNot: Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen risks hypercapnia and does not treat the existing red-cell excess.
Diuretics treat oedema; they would concentrate the blood further.
Anticoagulation is not the treatment for secondary polycythaemia.
Correcting hypoxaemia is part of the solution; stopping oxygen would make polycythaemia worse.

questions.stem: A tutor asks students to separate the pulmonary from the systemic features of COPD.
questions.leadIn: Which is an extrapulmonary (systemic) manifestation?
questions.explanation: Systemic effects include **skeletal muscle dysfunction**, weight loss, osteoporosis, raised inflammatory markers and salt and water retention. Muscle weakness limits exercise independently of FEV1.
whyNot: Goblet cell hyperplasia is an airway (pulmonary) change that causes sputum.
Hyperinflation is a pulmonary mechanical consequence of gas trapping.
Alveolar destruction is emphysema, a lung change.
Airway wall fibrosis is a pulmonary change causing premature airway closure.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: As-needed short-acting β2-agonist or short-acting antimuscarinic

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has mild COPD (FEV1 82% predicted) and gets breathless only when hurrying uphill. He has had no exacerbations.
items.explanation: Mild, intermittent symptoms need only **short-acting bronchodilators as needed** (step 1).

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman using salbutamol as needed is still limited by breathlessness. She has no history of atopy or variable symptoms, and her blood eosinophil count is normal.
items.explanation: With no asthmatic or steroid-responsive features, the next step is **dual long-acting bronchodilation (LABA + LAMA)**.

items.stem: A 61-year-old ex-smoker with COPD has hay fever, eczema and symptoms that vary a lot from week to week. He remains breathless on a short-acting inhaler.
items.explanation: Asthmatic or steroid-responsive features make **LABA + ICS** the preferred step 2 choice.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman on triple inhaled therapy, with good technique, still has four exacerbations a year. Her sputum is scanty and thin. Her team wants a long-term treatment proven to cut exacerbation frequency.
items.explanation: Two steps: scanty sputum makes a mucolytic (and a chronic bronchitis–targeted PDE4 inhibitor) less fitting. **Long-term macrolide (azithromycin)** reduces exacerbations in frequent exacerbators.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to define an acute exacerbation of COPD.
questions.leadIn: Which description fits best?
options: A worsening of symptoms with deterioration in lung function and health status
A fall in FEV1 of more than 12% on routine spirometry
Any upper respiratory viral infection in a COPD patient
New consolidation on the chest X-ray
An oxygen saturation below 92% at rest
questions.explanation: Davidson defines an exacerbation as an **increase in symptoms with deterioration in lung function and health status**. Clinically: more breathlessness, or more or purulent sputum.
whyNot: The 12% figure is a reversibility threshold, not a definition of exacerbation.
A viral infection is a trigger; it is only an exacerbation if symptoms worsen.
Consolidation indicates pneumonia, which may complicate but does not define an exacerbation.
Low saturation may accompany an exacerbation but is not its definition.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with COPD attends her annual review in autumn and asks about vaccines.
questions.leadIn: Which vaccination plan is recommended?
options: Annual influenza vaccine plus pneumococcal vaccination
No vaccines, because they trigger exacerbations
questions.explanation: Infections commonly trigger exacerbations, so every COPD patient should have **influenza vaccine every year** and **pneumococcal vaccination**.
whyNot: Omitting the yearly influenza vaccine leaves a major exacerbation trigger uncovered.
Influenza vaccine must be given every year, not every 5 years.
Vaccines prevent infective exacerbations; they are not a recognised trigger.
BCG is not part of routine COPD care.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old smoker has just had COPD confirmed on spirometry. The GP asks why a chest X-ray is still needed.
questions.leadIn: What is the main purpose of the chest X-ray in this setting?
options: To exclude other diagnoses such as lung cancer or heart failure and to look for bullae
To grade the severity of airflow obstruction
To confirm the diagnosis of COPD
To decide whether inhaled steroids are needed
questions.explanation: The CXR has **no reliable signs of severity** and may be normal even in advanced disease. It is essential to **exclude alternatives** (heart failure, lung cancer) and to detect **bullae**.
whyNot: Severity is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1, not by the radiograph.
Diagnosis requires spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.7).
Lung volumes (plethysmography) measure hyperinflation; the CXR is often normal.
ICS choice depends on exacerbation history, FEV1 and eosinophils, not the CXR.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His family ask about steroids.
questions.leadIn: Which steroid plan follows Davidson?
options: Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for about 10 days
Double his inhaled corticosteroid dose instead of systemic steroids
No steroids, because they worsen hypercapnia
questions.explanation: Davidson recommends **oral prednisolone 30 mg for 10 days** (shorter courses are acceptable), with bone protection if courses are repeated.
whyNot: Inhaled steroids are maintenance drugs and cannot replace systemic steroids in an exacerbation.
Maintenance oral steroids cause osteoporosis and muscle weakness and should be avoided.
Steroids improve symptoms and lung function in exacerbations; they do not worsen hypercapnia.
Prolonged IV steroids have no role and carry heavy side-effects.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a 30 pack-year history has had a chronic cough for 3 years. Pre-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.66. After salbutamol, FEV1/FVC is 0.68 and FEV1 rises by 90 mL (5%) to 71% of predicted.
questions.leadIn: What is the most accurate interpretation?
questions.explanation: **Step 1: is there obstruction?** The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.68, below 0.7, so yes. **Step 2: is it reversible?** A 90 mL (5%) rise is well short of the > 12% and > 200 mL needed, and far below the > 400 mL that suggests asthma. **Step 3: grade it.** A post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 71% falls in the 50–79% band, so this is **moderate COPD**. With symptoms and a smoking history, the diagnosis is secure.
whyNot: Mild needs FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted; his is 71%.
The bronchodilator response is minimal; asthma would typically show a large (> 400 mL) rise.
Severe is FEV1 30–49% predicted.
A post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.68 is obstructive.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with known CO2 retention is admitted with an exacerbation. She receives 28% Venturi oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral prednisolone. One hour later she is alert and coughing effectively. ABG: pH 7.31, PaCO2 8.4 kPa, PaO2 7.9 kPa, HCO3 32 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase oxygen to 60% via a reservoir mask
Start IV aminophylline and repeat gases in 6 hours
questions.explanation: **Step 1: read the gas.** The high bicarbonate shows chronic retention, and the pH below 7.35 with a high PaCO2 shows **acute on chronic respiratory acidosis**. **Step 2: check the timing.** This persists _after_ initial medical treatment and controlled oxygen. **Step 3: check suitability.** She is alert and can clear secretions, so she can protect her airway. That makes **NIV** the right step; started early it reduces intubation, treatment failure and death. Keep monitoring the ABG to judge the response.
whyNot: High-concentration oxygen in a CO2 retainer risks respiratory depression and worse acidosis.
IV aminophylline has limited evidence and arrhythmia risk, and delaying ventilatory support is unsafe.
Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications; she is alert and cooperative.
Doxapram has been largely superseded by NIV.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with COPD is stable on optimal therapy. ABGs on air 3 weeks apart both show PaO2 6.9 kPa. FEV1 is 1.1 L. He still smokes 10 cigarettes a day.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Prescribe LTOT for at least 15 hours a day now
Withhold LTOT and support him to stop smoking first
Prescribe LTOT only if his PaCO2 is normal
questions.explanation: **Step 1: does he meet the gas criterion?** Yes: PaO2 < 7.3 kPa on two stable samples 3 weeks apart, with FEV1 < 1.5 L. **Step 2: check the other conditions.** LTOT requires that the patient **has stopped smoking**; oxygen with cigarettes is a serious fire hazard. **Step 3: act.** Prioritise smoking cessation (the only measure that changes the natural history), then prescribe LTOT once he has stopped.
whyNot: Starting LTOT while he still smokes breaks a core prescribing condition and risks fire.
Short-burst oxygen is not LTOT, cannot provide the ≥ 15 h/day linked to the survival benefit, and is still unsafe while he smokes.
Night-only oxygen is not LTOT and would not apply while he smokes.
Davidson's criterion applies whatever the PaCO2.

questions.theme: Precipitants of acute deterioration in COPD
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with COPD gets worse after 2 days of a runny nose and sore throat. His sputum is unchanged and white, his temperature is normal and the CXR is clear.
items.explanation: Coryzal onset, unchanged sputum and a clear CXR fit a **viral** trigger; many exacerbations are viral.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with severe COPD is given 15 L/min oxygen through a reservoir mask by the ambulance crew. On arrival she is drowsy. Her PaCO2 has risen from a known baseline of 7.5 kPa to 10.2 kPa.
items.explanation: Two steps: a **known CO2 retainer** plus **uncontrolled high-flow oxygen**, then rising PaCO2 and drowsiness. High-concentration oxygen causes respiratory depression and worsening acidosis in these patients.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has become steadily more breathless over 2 weeks. He ran out of his inhalers a month ago because he could not afford a new prescription. There is no fever and the sputum is unchanged.
items.explanation: **Non-adherence to therapy** is one of the commonest causes of exacerbation.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with COPD, 9 days after a hip replacement, suddenly becomes breathless and tachycardic. Her sputum is unchanged and the CXR shows no new change.
items.explanation: Sudden breathlessness after surgery with a clear CXR and no change in sputum should prompt a search for **pulmonary embolism**, a mimic of exacerbation that must be excluded.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman who has never smoked has fixed airflow obstruction. Her brother had liver cirrhosis in his thirties.
items.explanation: Premature COPD in a **never-smoker** with a family history of liver disease calls for **alpha1-antitrypsin level and genotype**.

items.stem: A 63-year-old smoker with chronic productive cough and exertional breathlessness. His GP wants to confirm the diagnosis.
items.explanation: COPD is confirmed only by **post-bronchodilator spirometry** showing FEV1/FVC < 0.7.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD is being assessed for lung volume reduction surgery. The surgeons need to know how his emphysema is distributed.
items.explanation: **HRCT** characterises and quantifies emphysema, detects bullae better than the CXR, and guides LVRS.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD is plethoric and has headaches. His doctor wants to document the suspected complication.
items.explanation: A **full blood count** (haemoglobin, PCV) documents **secondary polycythaemia**.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with large bullae has lung volumes measured by helium dilution. They appear surprisingly small given how hyperinflated she looks.
items.explanation: Two steps: helium cannot equilibrate with poorly ventilated bullae, so it **under-estimates** volumes. **Body plethysmography** is preferred in severe COPD with bullae.

questions.stem: A student is comparing the two classic COPD phenotypes.
questions.leadIn: Which feature is typical of the "blue bloater" rather than the "pink puffer"?
options: Early hypercapnia with oedema and secondary polycythaemia
PaCO2 that stays normal until late disease
questions.explanation: Blue bloaters develop (or tolerate) **hypercapnia early**, become **oedematous** and develop **secondary polycythaemia**. Pink puffers are thin and breathless and keep a normal PaCO2 until late. In practice the two overlap.
whyNot: Thin and breathless describes the pink puffer.
A normal PaCO2 until late is the pink puffer pattern.
Pursed lips without cyanosis describes the pink puffer.
Predominant emphysema is the pink puffer; blue bloaters are bronchitis-predominant.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with COPD has more breathlessness and purulent sputum. He is not allergic to penicillin, and β-lactamase-producing organisms are uncommon in his area.
questions.leadIn: Which antibiotic choice is most appropriate?
options: No antibiotic, because exacerbations are always viral
questions.explanation: Increased purulence justifies antibiotics. Davidson advises a **simple regimen**: an **aminopenicillin** (e.g. amoxicillin), a tetracycline or a macrolide.
whyNot: Co-amoxiclav is reserved for regions where β-lactamase producers are common.
A broad-spectrum IV carbapenem is unnecessary for a simple community exacerbation.
Vancomycin covers Gram-positive organisms such as MRSA and is not used for routine exacerbations.
Many exacerbations are viral, but purulent sputum is a recognised indication for antibiotics.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the single best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman with COPD has needed several courses of oral prednisolone over the past year. After lifting a shopping bag she develops sudden mid-back pain. An X-ray shows a vertebral wedge fracture.
items.explanation: Two steps: COPD itself raises the prevalence of **osteoporosis**, and repeated steroid courses add to it. A low-trauma vertebral fracture is the result.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with long-standing severe COPD has a raised JVP, tender hepatomegaly and ankle oedema. The ECG shows tall P waves and right ventricular hypertrophy, and echo shows raised pulmonary artery pressure.
items.explanation: Raised pulmonary pressures with right-sided congestion and P pulmonale/RVH on ECG mean true **pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure** (cor pulmonale).

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD is well at a routine review. ABG on air: pH 7.38, PaCO2 7.8 kPa, PaO2 7.9 kPa, HCO3 34 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Raised PaCO2 with a **normal pH and high bicarbonate** is **chronic (compensated) type II respiratory failure**, a late complication for which COPD is the commonest cause.

questions.stem: Four patients with COPD exacerbations have pH 7.28–7.32 and a raised PaCO2 despite initial treatment.
questions.leadIn: In which patient is NIV contraindicated?
options: A man who is alert, cooperative and coughing effectively
A woman with GCS 8 who cannot clear copious secretions and is vomiting blood
A man with a respiratory rate of 32/min who is alert and using his accessory muscles
A woman with pneumonia on the CXR who is cooperative
A man with peripheral oedema who is alert
questions.explanation: NIV needs a patient who can **protect the airway** and cooperate. A depressed conscious level, inability to clear secretions and upper GI bleeding are all contraindications, so this patient needs intubation if appropriate.
whyNot: Alert, cooperative patients with respiratory acidosis are ideal NIV candidates.
Tachypnoea (respiratory rate > 30/min) with respiratory acidosis is an indication for NIV, not a contraindication.
Pneumonia as a reversible precipitant does not stop NIV in a cooperative patient.
Oedema is treated with diuretics and is not a contraindication to NIV.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a 40 pack-year history has known COPD. At review she has new finger clubbing. Spirometry is unchanged.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate interpretation of the clubbing?
options: It suggests another disease, such as lung cancer or fibrosis, and needs investigation
It is an expected sign of advanced COPD
questions.explanation: **Clubbing is not a feature of COPD.** Its appearance should trigger investigation for **lung cancer or fibrosis**.
whyNot: COPD does not cause clubbing at any stage.
Hypercapnia causes warm peripheries, a bounding pulse and flapping tremor, not clubbing.
Cor pulmonale causes raised JVP, hepatomegaly and oedema, not clubbing.
Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency causes early basal emphysema, not clubbing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD and a known raised bicarbonate is admitted with an exacerbation. Oxygen is being started.
questions.leadIn: What target oxygen saturation is appropriate?
questions.explanation: For patients **at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure**, controlled oxygen via a Venturi mask targets **SpO2 88–92%**. This corrects dangerous hypoxaemia without worsening acidosis.
whyNot: A target of 94% or above is for patients who do not retain CO2.
Aiming for 100% in a CO2 retainer risks respiratory depression and acidosis.
80–84% leaves him dangerously hypoxaemic.
Above 96% overshoots and risks hypercapnia.

ospe.identify: Gross specimen of emphysema: enlarged airspaces with loss of gas-exchange surface, compared with normal lung
PAS-stained bronchial mucosa with excess goblet cells: mucus hypersecretion of chronic bronchitis/COPD
COPD at the bedside: wasting, pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, leaning forward, accessory muscles, intercostal indrawing
Obstructive spirometry: slow prolonged exhalation, low FEV1/FVC and a scooped expiratory flow–volume loop (contrast with fibrosis)
HRCT with emphysema: large areas of low attenuation and lost lung architecture (here worst in the right lower lobe)
COPD chest X-ray: hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragms, enlarged retrosternal airspace
Venturi mask: a fixed-performance device for controlled oxygen (24%, 28%, 35%) in CO2 retainers
